title: My conclusion after a lot of testing: free public market data has no edge left for retail. Prove me wrong.
author: Ok_Map5721
selftext:
I spent a lot of time testing ideas on public data, the same exchange candles, funding rates and economic releases anyone can download for free. My honest conclusion so far is that there's nothing left in it for a retail trader after real costs. I'd genuinely like to be wrong, so here's my reasoning, and please tear it apart.

1. Anything simple is taken. MA crosses, RSI levels, breakouts, session opens. If it fits in one line and runs on free candles, thousands of people and plenty of bots have already tried it. What I kept finding was a small gross edge that costs ate completely.

2. Costs decide almost everything. One example I closed: rotating into small coins with high funding. About +5 bp a day gross, against roughly 14 bp a day in fees and spread.

3. Ideas with a real reason behind them still died. A month-end stock/bond rebalancing effect looked great over 20+ years, with an actual mechanism (funds have to rebalance). It fell apart on the period the original study didn't use.

4. The search fools you. Test 1,000 variants on the same data and the best one shows a t-stat around 3.7 on pure noise. Most public-data backtests posted here are the winner of a search like that, without the count.

5. AI makes it worse. It churns out strategies faster than ever, but it has already seen the history it's tested on, and everyone with a subscription is running the same search.

What would change my mind: something built only on free public data that made money after real fees and slippage, on a period you didn't look at while building it, and that you can explain WHY it should keep working. You don't have to share the setup. Just the market, roughly how long it's held up, and why you think it persists.

If it exists, I want to know where I went wrong.

comments.author: Flimsy-Rip2459
comments.body: Depends what asset class your trading. I suggest you take a look at commodities where data is disparate and already across various places. Gold in particular has both physical,paper, geopolitical, economic aspects where data comes in to play. I've had luck pulling data from the API on goldsquawk that I then feed I to my trading bot...but it's taken some screwing with it to get it to work.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
commodities is a fair point, data there is scattered across physical, paper, positioning and reports, so less of it is already priced from one clean feed. that's probably the most interesting answer so far.

curious about two things: when you say you've had luck, is that live results after costs over a decent number of trades, or still backtest? and is the edge in reacting to the news faster, or in interpreting it better? the first one is usually a race you lose to people with faster feeds, the second one can last.

replies.author: Flimsy-Rip2459
replies.body: Only moved I to live testing around 3 weeks ago but am seeing early signs of success with all costs included... It's definitely not speed I'm going for it's the interpretation side.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
interpretation is the side I'd bet on too. one thing that helped me at this stage: log every signal the bot reads from the news, including the ones it didn't trade, with the price at that moment. after a few months you can check whether the trades it took beat the ones it skipped, and whether it beats random entries on the same days. three weeks of gold can easily be one regime, especially with how gold's been moving.

would genuinely like to hear how it looks in 3-6 months, feel free to DM.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
Point 2 matches what I saw the most. I had a strategy that looked fine on clean fills, and once I added commission and volatility-based slippage most of the small wins were just gone.

Did you try the same ideas on slower timeframes though? Feels like that's where free data still has a chance, since costs stop eating everything.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
yeah, volatility-based slippage is the one that kills most small wins, flat slippage hides it.

and yes, slower is where I've had more luck too, costs stop being the whole story. the catch I keep hitting there is fewer trades, so it takes much longer to tell an edge from a lucky stretch, and a lot of what survives turns out to be paid for holding a risk, trend or carry, rather than a real edge. still worth it, just slower to prove.

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: The "paid for holding a risk" part is a good point, I didn't think of it like that. I guess it's still fine to trade, as long as you know it's trend or carry and not some edge only you found.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
exactly, the only danger is sizing it like an edge. a premium can lag for years and still be fine, so you size it for the long ugly stretch, not for the backtest.

you've been one of the most useful people in my threads, if you ever want to compare notes properly, DM me. and feel free to follow.

comments.author: ATKInvestments
comments.body: All indicators are 50/50. You have to build a bias. Decay is real. Understanding Decay is were you can find a bias because the Decay is what creates the cycle. There's a massive domino effect. The other approach is fundamentals. I know this isn't new info. But keep changing your approach to what's really not working as you gain more knowledge. It's a long process of elimination. If I stated something new that was working for me? It would immediately Decay from everyone trying it.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: agree that the elimination part is most of the job. I'm curious what you mean by decay creating the cycle, is it the edge itself fading as people pile in, or something like volatility or momentum decaying in a way you can time? a concrete example of the domino effect would help, even an old dead one.

comments.author: Ok-Cake9189
comments.body:
My testing results have been similar to yours. I curently have claude connected to tradestation live data during market hours and paper trading about 20 strategies. Separately I have started a daily jev report that scans for headlines, fed events, etc. and gives me a daily.....well shit, I'll let Claude tell you:
What the daily JEV report is: a forecast card, made each weekday morning before the open, that estimates what kind of day SPY is likely to have. It's tracking only and never places a trade.
What goes in
The calendar: Fed meetings, CPI, jobs reports, options expiration, month start and end, holidays.
Market mood: the VIX "fear gauges," dealer gamma (whether big options dealers tend to calm moves or amplify them), and whether SPY is above or below its 200-day average.
Earnings: which big AI and megacap companies report today or in the next 5 trading days.
News: overnight headlines from CNBC, MarketWatch, the Fed and Google News, plus the stories Tear posts on Trading Edge. Jev sees only the stories themselves, not Tear's opinions or price levels.
What comes out: odds for about 9 yes/no questions, such as: will today be a big-range day, a trend day, a choppy day, or open with a gap up or down? Four forecasters answer side by side:
Base rate: "a normal day," straight from 20 years of history.
Rules: history adjusted for proven events. Fed days are the strongest one, with about 2–3× the normal odds of a big day.
Jev: an AI that sees the calendar only.
Jev + news: the same AI, also reading the headlines.
Why it might be useful: if the card can reliably flag the big days in advance, you could use it to size down, sit out, or pick a different strategy on those days. The catch is that history shows over half of big days have no scheduled event. The news layer is the bet that headlines can catch some of those.
How we'll test it: every day, each forecast is graded against what actually happened, using a standard accuracy score. After 60+ graded days we compare the four. If Jev + news doesn't beat the plain history numbers, it isn't adding anything.
Where I think the plan has gaps:
60 days is probably too short to tell. Big days happen only about 1 day in 7, and a Fed meeting comes about every 6 weeks. In 60 days we'd see only a handful of the days that matter, so a "win" could easily be luck. Treat day 60 as a first look. A real verdict likely needs around 6 months, or a backtest on old headlines (that's the GDELT step on the to-do list).
We haven't decided what you'd actually do with a forecast. Better odds only pay off if they change a trading action. We should write down now what the card would change, for example "if big-range odds are above X%, halve the size on strategy Y." Then we can test that action and not just the accuracy score.
Jev called "chop" on every early test day. Chop is the most common day type, so always guessing it scores decently while telling you nothing. We should check that Jev's odds actually move from day to day.

End Claude, start human again:
Because the backtesting over long peeiods of time has so far found to strat worth automating, but they all won simetimes,  Im thinking that maybe I can create a tool that eventually might give me an idea of under what conditions certain strats have the best probabilty of beating a buy and hild in an index. I'll run a few months of data, see what happens.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
this is one of the most careful setups I've seen here, and the "what action does the card change" point is the key one. accuracy alone can look great while being useless.

one thing that might help with the short sample: score it on the action, not just the odds. like "half size on flagged big-range days" vs "always full size" on the same strategies, same days. and for the base rate, a simple volatility forecast from recent realized vol (yesterday + last week + last month) is a tough benchmark, often tougher than history alone.

I'd really like to compare notes on this, I've been looking at range forecasting for sizing too. DM me if you're up for it, and feel free to follow.

comments.author: SethEllis
comments.body: Momentum is a well studied strategy that relies on public data.  You probably need to look at higher timeframe portfolio level strategies.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: fair, cross-sectional momentum at portfolio level is probably the strongest public-data answer in this thread. I'd file it under premium rather than edge though, it's well documented, paid for sitting through brutal momentum crashes like 2009, and it's gotten thinner as more money chases it. still worth having, just with eyes open about the crashes.
